question: What is a lock in a DBMS?
ideal_answer: A lock is a variable associated with a data item that describes the status of the item with respect to the operations that can be applied to it. There is one lock for each data item in the database. Locks are used to synchronize the access by concurrent transactions to the database items.

question: What is the two-phase locking protocol?
ideal_answer: A transaction follows the two-phase locking protocol if all its locking operations (read_lock, write_lock) precede the first unlock operation in the transaction. Such a transaction has an expanding (growing) phase, during which new locks can be acquired but none can be released. It then has a shrinking phase, during which existing locks can be released but no new locks can be acquired.

question: What is data item granularity and why does choosing it matter?
ideal_answer: Data item granularity is the size of the data item that a lock applies to, such as a record, a disk block, a file or the whole database. Choosing the right granularity is important because it affects concurrency, i.e. how many transactions can run at the same time. It also affects overhead, i.e. the system effort needed to manage locks.

question: What is the phantom phenomenon?
ideal_answer: The phantom phenomenon occurs when a transaction retrieves a set of rows satisfying a condition and another transaction inserts or deletes rows that also meet that condition. This leads to inconsistent query results because the retrieved data changes during the transaction's execution. For example, if T1 reads all rows with salary > 5000 and T2 inserts a row with salary 6000, T1 sees an extra phantom row when it re-runs the query.

question: What is a certify lock in multiversion two-phase locking?
ideal_answer: A certify lock is the third type of lock that multiversion two-phase locking (MV2PL) adds to read and write locks. Before a transaction T can commit, it must get a certify lock on every item it updated. The certify lock ensures that no other transaction is reading the old version while T commits.

question: Why is the binary locking scheme too restrictive, and what is used instead?
ideal_answer: Binary locking is too restrictive because at most one transaction can hold a lock on a given item. Read operations on the same item by different transactions are not conflicting, so several transactions should be allowed to read the same item at once. A transaction that writes an item still needs exclusive access to it. This is achieved with a multiple-mode lock called shared/exclusive (read/write) locks.

question: Why can two-phase locking limit the amount of concurrency in a schedule?
ideal_answer: Under two-phase locking a transaction T may not be able to release an item X after it is done with it if T must lock another item Y later. Alternatively, T must lock Y before it needs it so that it can release X. Meanwhile other transactions that want X or Y are forced to wait even though T is done with X or not yet using Y. This is the price for guaranteeing serializability of all schedules without having to check the schedules themselves.

question: What is Thomas's write rule?
ideal_answer: Thomas's write rule is a modification of the basic timestamp ordering algorithm that rejects fewer write operations but does not enforce conflict serializability. When T issues write_item(X): if read_TS(X) > TS(T), T is aborted and rolled back and the operation is rejected. If write_TS(X) > TS(T), the write is not executed but processing continues, because the write is already outdated and obsolete. Otherwise the write is executed and write_TS(X) is set to TS(T).

question: How does the two-phase commit protocol work?
ideal_answer: Two-phase commit ensures atomicity in distributed transactions: all participating nodes either commit or abort together, even in the presence of failures. In the prepare phase, the coordinator sends a PREPARE request to all participants, asking whether they can commit. In the commit/abort phase, if all participants reply Yes the coordinator sends COMMIT and they commit, but if any participant replies No the coordinator sends ABORT and all participants abort. Each participant logs the commit or abort and releases any locks held for the transaction.

question: How do strict 2PL and multiversion 2PL each avoid cascading aborts?
ideal_answer: Strict 2PL releases all exclusive (write) locks only after the transaction commits or aborts. As a result, a transaction only reads committed data, which avoids cascading rollbacks. Multiversion 2PL lets other transactions read the old, committed version while a transaction writes a new version. Because transactions only read committed data there, a rollback does not cause a chain of aborts.

question: Which concurrency control techniques in this unit avoid deadlocks, and why?
ideal_answer: Timestamp-ordering techniques do not use locks, so deadlocks cannot occur. Conservative 2PL acquires all locks before the transaction begins execution, which avoids deadlocks but can cause delays due to pre-locking. Strict timestamp ordering does not cause deadlock either, because a transaction T waits for another transaction T' only if TS(T) > TS(T').

question: During recovery, what happens to transactions that were active at the time of failure versus those that had committed, and which log images are used?
ideal_answer: Transactions that were active at the time of failure are undone (rolled back) using the before images in the transaction log, restoring the data to its state before the transaction started. Transactions that had committed before the failure are redone using the after images from the log, so that their updates are applied. The before image is the value of a data item before it is updated, and the after image is its value after it has been updated.

question: In multiple granularity locking, is an IX lock compatible with an S lock, and is an IS lock compatible with an SIX lock?
ideal_answer: No, IX is not compatible with S. Yes, IS is compatible with SIX. In the compatibility table, IS is compatible with every lock mode except X.

question: In the example of transactions T1 and T2 that do not obey two-phase locking, with initial values X=20 and Y=30, what are the results of the serial schedules and of the nonserializable schedule S?
ideal_answer: The serial schedule T1 followed by T2 gives X=50 and Y=80. The serial schedule T2 followed by T1 gives X=70 and Y=50. The nonserializable schedule S that uses locks gives X=50 and Y=50.

question: In multiversion timestamp ordering, X has versions X1 (write_TS=5, read_TS=10) and X2 (write_TS=15, read_TS=20). What happens when T3 with TS=18 tries to write X, and when T4 with TS=25 tries to write X?
ideal_answer: For T3 the latest suitable version is X2, because write_TS(X2)=15 <= 18. But read_TS(X2)=20 > 18, so there is a conflict and T3 is aborted. For T4 the suitable version is also X2 and read_TS(X2)=20 <= 25, so there is no conflict. A new version X3 is created with write_TS(X3)=25 and read_TS(X3)=25.

question: Under basic timestamp ordering, transaction T with TS(T)=10 issues read_item(X). What happens if write_TS(X)=12, and what happens if write_TS(X)=8?
ideal_answer: If write_TS(X)=12 then write_TS(X) > TS(T), meaning a younger transaction has already written X before T could read it. In that case T is aborted and rolled back and the read is rejected. If write_TS(X)=8 then write_TS(X) <= TS(T), so read_item(X) is executed and read_TS(X) is set to the larger of TS(T) and the current read_TS(X).

question: How does strict timestamp ordering differ from basic timestamp ordering?
ideal_answer: Basic timestamp ordering aborts and rolls back a transaction whenever an operation would violate the timestamp order, and its schedules are not guaranteed to be recoverable, so cascading rollback can occur. In strict timestamp ordering, a read_item(X) or write_item(X) by T with TS(T) > write_TS(X) is delayed until the transaction that wrote X has committed or aborted. This makes the schedules both strict (for easy recoverability) and conflict serializable.

question: How does validation-based (optimistic) concurrency control differ from two-phase locking?
ideal_answer: In validation (optimistic) concurrency control, transactions execute without locking resources, assuming conflicts are rare. Before committing, a validation phase checks whether the transaction conflicts with others; it commits if it passes and aborts otherwise. In 2PL, transactions acquire locks on resources so that no conflicts occur during execution, which gives strict consistency but may cause delays due to lock contention. Validation is suitable for low-contention environments.

question: What is Boyce-Codd Normal Form (BCNF)?
ideal_answer: A relation is in Boyce-Codd Normal Form if, for every non-trivial functional dependency X -> Y, X is a superkey of the relation. BCNF is a stricter version of Third Normal Form.

question: How does Oracle implement multiversion read consistency using undo segments?
ideal_answer: Oracle uses undo data to provide multiversion read consistency. When a query reads a block that was changed after the query began, Oracle reconstructs the older version of the data from the undo segments. Readers therefore see a consistent snapshot as of the query's start and do not block writers.
